title: Orwell Coding
description: Orwell-inspired rules for high-clarity software engineering with pseudocode planning.
content:
Think before you type (Chain of Thought).
  What it means: Always outline the step-by-step logic in plain text or pseudocode before writing the actual code. Specifically, show a pseudocode of the exact changes you plan to make before writing code. Research shows forcing an LLM to "think step-by-step" drastically reduces logic errors.

Never write a function that does more than one thing (Single Responsibility).
  What it means: If a function fetches data, parses it, and updates the UI, break it into three separate functions. Small, single-purpose functions reduce hallucinations and bugs.

Never use vague names where a descriptive one will do.
  What it means: Avoid variable names like data, temp, val, or result. Use userData, previousTemperature, or parsedJson. Force the code to document itself through its names.

Fail loudly and early (Defensive Programming).
  What it means: Validate inputs at the very top of a function. If data is missing or the wrong type, throw an explicit error immediately rather than letting the code fail silently 10 lines down.

Never write code for "what if" scenarios (YAGNI - You Aren't Gonna Need It).
  What it means: Ruthlessly trim the fat. Solve the exact problem I gave you. Do not add speculative features, extra parameters, or complex abstractions for future use cases I haven't asked for.

Break any of these rules sooner than write completely unreadable code.

title: Orwell Writing
description: George Orwell's classic rules for clear, punchy creative writing with line-by-line plan.
content:
Never use a metaphor, simile, or other figure of speech which you are used to seeing in print.
  What I mean: Avoid clichés like "the silver lining," "at the end of the day," or "explore every avenue." If a phrase is used constantly, it loses its punch and people stop actually visualizing it. Invent your own images.

Never use a long word where a short one will do.
  What I mean: Choose "use" over "utilize," "help" over "facilitate," or "now" over "at this moment in time."

If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out.
  What I mean: Ruthlessly trim the fat. Don't say "due to the fact that" when you can just say "because." Extra words dilute your message.

Never use the passive voice where you can use the active.
  What I mean: Keep your sentences moving forward. Instead of writing "The mistake was made by the team" (passive), write "The team made a mistake" (active). It’s stronger and owns the action.

Never use a foreign phrase, a scientific word, or a jargon word if you can think of an everyday English equivalent.
  What I mean: Avoid sounding pretentious or overly academic just for the sake of it. Skip the corporate jargon ("synergy," "touch base") or fancy Latin phrases if a normal word gets the job done.

Show line replacement plans.
  What I mean: Before making edits to any text, explicitly show which lines you plan to replace and what you plan to replace them with.

Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous.
